questions_asked:
In wealthy Western countries (the US, Australia, Western Europe) with low, stable
HIV rates, when people say "no new AIDS programs added," do they mean HIV cases
would keep growing, stay flat, or slowly decline as existing clinic access and
condom use run their course?

In the worst-hit African countries (e.g. South Africa, Zimbabwe, Zambia) that in
the mid-1990s had HIV rates around 10–25 percent and were still rising: with no
new AIDS programs at all, what did people at the time expect — would total HIV
cases keep climbing for years, level off around some ceiling, or start to fall
once the infection pool ran out of easy partners?

A new preventive HIV vaccine only protects the people who actually get it
(infants or adults). In a country where many adults are already infected, would
widespread vaccination of newborns and young people mainly slow the growth of
new infections, or would it also shrink the existing number of infected people
over time?

For a group of about six poor, high-burden countries (southern/eastern African
plus India, Brazil), what realistic total foreign-aid money per year would donors
worldwide actually make available for HIV/AIDS between 2006 and 2050 — roughly
how many billions of dollars per year for all six combined, and would it stay
roughly steady, grow with world wealth, or taper off over time?

When a country with high HIV prevalence puts a large share of its infected
people on antiretroviral drugs, in practice what dominates the effect on the
total number of infected people: they live longer (so the infected count stays
up or rises), the drugs lower their ability to pass the virus on, or both — and
which effect is usually the bigger one?

As of the mid-2000s, when working in HIV research, what year did people realistically expect a preventive HIV vaccine would first be ready for wide use in poor countries — somewhere around 2015, 2020, 2030, or not at all before then? And roughly how many years would it take to vaccinate a meaningful share of a large population once it existed?

Working in HIV vaccine research in the mid-2000s, when a preventive HIV vaccine
finally became available, what level of protection did people realistically
expect it to give a vaccinated person — roughly what percent chance it would
keep them from getting HIV — and would that protection last for a person's whole
life, or fade and need a booster shot every few years?

In large AIDS-drug programs run in poor African countries (the DOTS/directly-observed kind), in practice what share of the people on treatment actually stay on their drugs faithfully — above about 90 percent of doses taken — versus dropping below that level, when the program is at full scale?

You are advising the UN on limited HIV/AIDS money in 2006. One choice is to spend
it now treating today's patients with AIDS drugs; the other is to invest some of
it in speeding up a vaccine that may not exist for 15–20 years. In practice, what
would most experienced AIDS program people recommend — how roughly should the
money be split between treating now and betting on the future vaccine?

Once a drug-resistant strain of AIDS appears among people on treatment, in
practice how does it spread through the wider population — does it mainly
re-infect the same treated group (and die out when those patients are dropped),
or does it pass on to untreated people the same way ordinary HIV does and keep
going even after the original patient is no longer on drugs?
expert_answers: Stay flat to slowly declining. In wealthy Western countries HIV incidence has been roughly stable or gently falling since the late 1990s, sustained by existing prevention (condom use, testing, harm reduction) and near-universal ARV access. "No new programs" means no additional scale-up, not withdrawal of current services, so the baseline trajectory continues: prevalence may drift slightly upward as ARV extends survival, while new infections stay flat or edge down. Growth is not the expected reading.

Keep climbing for years, then level off — not fall quickly. The mid-1990s expectation was continued steep growth in total infections for at least a decade or more, driven by high incidence in young adults and the long lag between infection and death. A ceiling was expected eventually, but a high one (adult prevalence plateauing roughly in the 20–30% range in the worst-hit southern African countries), reached mainly through saturation of the susceptible population and behavior change, not through the infection pool "running out of partners." A rapid decline was not the expected reading; absent programs, prevalence was projected to stay near its peak for a long time because ARV was not available and mortality only slowly reduced the infected pool.

Mainly slow the growth of new infections; it would not shrink the existing infected pool. A preventive vaccine does nothing for people already infected — they remain infected and, absent treatment, continue to progress and die at the existing rate. Vaccinating newborns and young people reduces the rate at which susceptible people become newly infected, so cumulative infections grow more slowly and prevalence can eventually fall as the unvaccinated infected cohort ages and dies out. But the number of currently infected people declines only through that same background mortality, not because of the vaccine. Any shrinkage of the infected pool over time comes from deaths and the aging-out of the infected cohort, not from vaccination itself.

Roughly **$5–15 billion per year** for all six combined in the early years (2006–2010), rising over time. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise figure.

Realistic trajectory:
- **2006–2010:** ~$5–10B/yr globally for HIV/AIDS, of which the six countries would capture a large share (Africa plus India/Brazil were the dominant recipients). Call it ~$3–8B/yr for the six.
- **2010–2020:** scale-up era; global HIV/AIDS aid peaked around **$8–10B/yr** (PEPFAR ~$5–7B, Global Fund ~$3–4B, plus other bilateral/multilateral). The six combined plausibly ~$6–10B/yr.
- **2020–2050:** roughly **steady in real terms, growing slowly with world wealth at best, and more likely flat-to-tapering** in per-year terms. Donor fatigue, competing priorities, and the epidemiological transition (falling incidence) argue against continued growth; a plateau in the **$5–15B/yr** range for the six is the reasonable central expectation.

So: order of magnitude **~$10B/yr**, roughly steady to mildly growing early, then flat or tapering — not compounding upward indefinitely.

Both effects are real, and in practice the survival effect usually dominates the count of infected people.

- **Survival effect (bigger for the infected count):** ARV sharply cuts AIDS mortality, so infected people live for decades instead of dying within years. This keeps the infected pool large and can make measured prevalence *rise*, even as new infections fall. In high-prevalence settings this is the dominant driver of the total infected number.
- **Transmission-reduction effect (smaller, but real):** Suppressing viral load lowers infectiousness substantially — near-zero transmission when viral suppression is good. This reduces *new* infections, which eventually shrinks the pool, but only slowly and only if coverage and adherence are high.

Net: in the first 10–20 years of a large-scale ARV rollout, longer survival dominates, so the total infected count stays flat or rises. The prevention benefit shows up later as fewer new infections, and only overtakes the survival effect over multi-decade horizons.

Around **2020** was the realistic mid-2000s expectation for a preventive HIV vaccine ready for wide use in poor countries — with wide uncertainty, commonly quoted as a 10–15 year horizon (so roughly 2015–2020), and many researchers privately doubted anything before 2020. "Not before 2030" was a minority pessimistic view; "by 2015" was the optimistic tail, not the central expectation. The 2003–2005 consensus was that vaccine development was scientifically stalled (no correlate of protection, the failed gp120 trials), so a licensed product was seen as a long way off.

For rollout speed: once a vaccine existed, reaching a meaningful share of a large population would take roughly **5–15 years**. Newborn/EPI-based delivery could scale relatively fast (a few years to reach high infant coverage, since the delivery platform already exists), but adult coverage would be much slower — building the delivery capacity to immunize a large fraction of adults in a poor country typically takes a decade or more. So: vaccine ~2020, meaningful population coverage ~5–15 years after that.

Realistic mid-2000s expectation: a **partially protective** vaccine, roughly **50–60% reduction in the chance of acquiring HIV** per exposure — not 90%+. The field's stated goal (the "50% efficacy" benchmark used in trial design) was a vaccine at least half-effective; anything near sterilizing immunity was considered unlikely and not the working assumption.

Duration: **not lifelong**. The expectation was **waning protection over roughly 3–5 years**, requiring periodic boosters — analogous to existing vaccines that need re-dosing. A one-shot, lifetime vaccine was the hope, not the assumption. So model it as ~50% efficacy, decaying over a few years, with booster doses needed to sustain protection.

At full scale in poor African programs, roughly **60–80% of patients stay above ~90% adherence**; the remaining **20–40% fall below** at some point. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise figure.

Key qualifications:
- **Trial and pilot settings** do much better — often 90%+ above threshold — because of intensive counseling, monitoring, and selection of motivated patients.
- **Routine full-scale rollout** is worse: adherence commonly drops to the 60–80% range, with a meaningful minority (roughly 20–40%) below 90% at any given time, and loss-to-follow-up (patients who simply stop showing up) is a large part of that.
- Adherence also **decays over time on treatment** — early months are good, then it slips as patients feel well and the regimen becomes routine.

So for a model at full scale, assuming something like **one-quarter to one-third of treated patients fall below 90% adherence** is realistic; assuming near-universal high adherence is not.

Most experienced AIDS program people in 2006 would recommend spending the large majority now on treatment and proven prevention, with only a modest share on vaccine R&D — roughly **80–90% to treatment/care, 10–20% to vaccine research**, and even that vaccine share mostly through existing global R&D channels rather than country programs.

Reasoning: treatment need was immediate, visible, and politically unavoidable (millions dying, ARV access pressure), while a vaccine was 15–20 years off with no guarantee of success. The standard view was that you cannot ethically divert large sums from people dying now to a speculative future product. Vaccine R&D was seen as a global public good best funded by wealthy governments and foundations, not by poor-country AIDS budgets.

The main exception: a small number argued for more front-loaded vaccine investment precisely because it is the only long-run exit from the epidemic, and because R&D has increasing returns if it pulls the date forward. But that was the minority position. So: treat now dominates; vaccine gets a real but minority share.

It passes on to untreated people the same way ordinary HIV does, and keeps going after the original patient is dropped.

Resistant strains are still HIV: they transmit sexually, perinatally, and through blood, with essentially the same transmission routes and efficiency as wild-type virus. So a resistant strain arising in one poorly adherent patient does not stay confined to the treated group — it enters the general susceptible population and spreads onward through ordinary transmission chains. Dropping or switching the original patient removes that one person from the treated pool but does nothing to the infections already seeded elsewhere.

The one qualification: resistant strains often carry a **fitness cost** — reduced replicative capacity relative to wild-type — so in the absence of drug pressure they can be outcompeted and decline in frequency over time. But they do not simply die out with the original patient; they persist and transmit, and where ARV coverage is widespread they retain a selective advantage because newly infected people are likely to be put on the same first-line drugs. That is why transmitted resistance accumulates rather than self-limiting.
